title: Given a `List<Employee>`, find, for each department, the single employee who earns the most, producing a `Map<String, Employee>`. Use `groupingBy` with `Collectors.collectingAndThen(maxBy(...), Optional::get)`.
shortTitle: Group employees by department, then get the employee with the highest salary in each department

s1_definition.profdef: `groupingBy(classifier, downstream)` with `Collectors.maxBy(comparator)` as the downstream produces `Map<String, Optional<Employee>>`, because a group's maximum is wrapped in an Optional. Wrapping that with `Collectors.collectingAndThen(maxBy(...), Optional::get)` unwraps each Optional, giving a clean `Map<String, Employee>` since every existing group is guaranteed non-empty.
s1_definition.analogy: Priya wants the top earner in each department — the "department champion". For every department tray she looks through the cards and keeps the one with the biggest salary. The maxBy downstream picks that champion per department, and collectingAndThen just takes it out of its wrapper box.
s1_definition.oneliner: `groupingBy(dept, collectingAndThen(maxBy(by salary), Optional::get))` gives the top earner per department.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `groupingBy(classifier, downstream)` with `Collectors.maxBy(comparator)` as the downstream produces `Map<String, Optional<Employee>>`, because a group's maximum is wrapped in an Optional. Wrapping that with `Collectors.collectingAndThen(maxBy(...), Optional::get)` unwraps each Optional, giving a clean `Map<String, Employee>` since every existing group is guaranteed non-empty.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Priya wants the top earner in each department — the "department champion". For every department tray she looks through the cards and keeps the one with the biggest salary. The maxBy downstream picks that champion per department, and collectingAndThen just takes it out of its wrapper box.

**One line to remember:** `groupingBy(dept, collectingAndThen(maxBy(by salary), Optional::get))` gives the top earner per department.

sections.s2_technical:
`Collectors.maxBy(comparator)` reduces a group to its maximum element according to the comparator and, because a reduction with no identity can be empty, returns an `Optional`. As the downstream of groupingBy you get `Map<String, Optional<Employee>>`. The comparator here is `Comparator.comparing(Employee::getSalary)`, so maxBy keeps the highest-salary employee.

To avoid the awkward Optional values I wrap the whole downstream in `Collectors.collectingAndThen(maxBy(...), Optional::get)`. `collectingAndThen` runs a collector and then applies a finishing function to its result. Here the finisher is `Optional::get`, which is safe because groupingBy only creates a key when at least one element fell into that group, so the Optional is always present.

A senior point: `Optional::get` is safe only under that guarantee. If I built the map differently — for instance starting from a fixed list of all possible departments — a department with no employees would produce an empty Optional and `get` would throw, so there I would use `orElse(null)` or filter. For ties in salary, maxBy keeps the last maximum it encounters by default; if I needed a deterministic tie-break I would add `thenComparing` to the comparator.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India runs a quarterly "top performer by department" recognition and needs the single highest earner in each department. Scanning each department manually is slow. This is exactly how maxBy as a downstream works — it reduces each department group to its top earner.

Problem 2 — The team dislikes handling Optional values scattered across the map. This is exactly why collectingAndThen with Optional::get is used — it unwraps every value to a plain Employee because each group is guaranteed non-empty.

The code defines `Employee`, a `RecognitionService` with `topEarnerByDepartment`, and a demo.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: IT Rajesh 95000 and Amit 120000; Finance Priya 250000 and Sneha 180000.

Step 1: Employees are grouped into IT and Finance.

Step 2: Within IT, maxBy compares 95000 and 120000 and keeps Amit, wrapped as `Optional.of(Amit)`.

Step 3: Within Finance, maxBy keeps Priya at 250000, wrapped as `Optional.of(Priya)`.

Step 4: `collectingAndThen` applies `Optional::get` to each value, unwrapping to plain Employees.

Step 5: The TreeMap yields alphabetical keys.

```
INFO: Finance top earner -> Priya (250000.0)
INFO: IT top earner -> Amit (120000.0)
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: IT[Rajesh/95k, Amit/120k], Finance[Priya/250k, Sneha/180k]
    │ groupingBy(dept, collectingAndThen(maxBy(salary), Optional::get))
    ▼
  per group reduce to max:
    ├─ IT      → Optional.of(Amit/120k)  --get--> Amit
    └─ Finance → Optional.of(Priya/250k) --get--> Priya
    ▼
  TreeMap<String,Employee>
    ▼
  Output: {Finance:Priya, IT:Amit}
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
To find the top earner in each department I group by department and use `Collectors.maxBy` with a salary comparator as the downstream. Because maxBy is a reduction with no identity it returns an Optional, so a plain groupingBy with maxBy gives a Map of department to Optional of Employee, which is awkward to consume.

To clean that up I wrap the downstream in `Collectors.collectingAndThen(maxBy(...), Optional::get)`. collectingAndThen runs a collector and then applies a finishing function, and here the finisher Optional::get unwraps each result to a plain Employee, giving a tidy Map of department to Employee.

The safety point I always make is that Optional::get is only safe here because groupingBy never creates a key for an empty group, so the Optional is always present. In my banking project at the National Bank of India this produced the quarterly top-performer-by-department list for recognition. I note that if the keys had instead come from a fixed list of all possible departments, a department with no employees would produce an empty Optional and get would throw, so there I would finish with orElse null or filter instead, and I would add a thenComparing tie-break if the business needed a deterministic winner when two salaries tie.
